doc.title: Don Menza and Sam Noto interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 28, 1997

title: Menza's brief stay with Kenton and Kenton's legacy
summary: Menza quit Kenton after two nights because it did not swing; talk of ghost bands, the library and the all-star band Noto joined.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: I don’t remember him putting that down—
The only thing I remember him putting down was country-western.

Oh no, he talked about opera and all that, he hated it man. Yeah. And yet it had a lot to do with, his concept was very much based on that classical sort of structure. But he was a sweetheart. I know I worked with the band a short time and I mean a very short time, I had left Maynard’s band to go with Stan Kenton, and the second night on the band I gave my notice. It didn’t swing.

Yes. And after Maynard’s band it was such a letdown for me, that I called Maynard, I tried to get my job back and Maynard was furious with me for leaving. And Stan was very sweet. He says, “I understand perfectly.” And I didn’t tell him it ain’t swinging, I said, “This isn’t what I wanted to do.” And I told him I said, “I have the greatest deal of respect for you,” and we remained friends to the day he died.
It’s also interesting that he left, from what I read, he left instructions that he did not want a ghost band.
He did not want a ghost band. And it’s happening all over the world.

Well they call them “tributes” though. He willed his whole library to North Texas State. So that’s where all the music is. But there are copies all over the place now, just run it through the machine.
Well his music was pretty popular with the college bands.
It was popular then but I mean his music was popular. It was a big time band in the late ‘40s, early ‘50s, it was huge.

Well the band, when I joined it was an all-star band. It was Lee Konitz, Zoot Sims and all those people were on that band. And that was — Conte, and then that was close to a swinging band also, because those were all pretty heavy jazz players. Frank Rosolino was on the band.
